idiom_name: Task race against Task.sleep / DispatchSemaphore.wait(timeout:) / URLSession budgets
implementation_notes: The standard library ships no timeout combinator: Task cancellation is a cooperative boolean (isCancelled, checkCancellation, withTaskCancellationHandler) that is only observed where the code looks, so a deadline is assembled either from a task group racing the operation against Task.sleep, or by using the first-party primitive that already carries one - DispatchSemaphore.wait(timeout:) returning .timedOut, and URLSessionConfiguration.timeoutIntervalForRequest/timeoutIntervalForResource for HTTP. Cancelling the group sets the flag but does not stop an uncooperative operation, and because withThrowingTaskGroup must await all children before it returns, such an operation turns the timeout back into an unbounded wait. Nothing replaces the structure here, so the race-and-cancel helper is written by hand (or taken from a package such as swift-async-algorithms).
pitfalls: Cancellation is cooperative and the group still awaits its children: an operation that never checks Task.isCancelled keeps the scope alive, so the timeout does not actually bound the wall-clock time.
DispatchSemaphore.wait(timeout:) blocks the calling thread and must not run on the main actor, and its .timedOut result has to be distinguished from .success.

URLSessionConfiguration.timeoutIntervalForRequest is reset whenever new data arrives, so it bounds the gap between packets rather than the total request; timeoutIntervalForResource is the overall budget.
A Task.sleep-based timer running in a detached task is not joined, so a fire-and-forget timeout task leaks unless it is cancelled or awaited.
